For example the syrup made from raisins, which the Arabs still today call دِبْس [dibs]; even in our own age so much of it is sent every year from the region of Hebron to Egypt as three hundred camels can carry, as Shaw writes in his Travels, p. 293 of the German version, note. Of this syrup [III, 375] Russell, in the Natural History of Aleppo, p. 20: the juice of the Grapes is sometimes thikened in a substance, that hath the appearance of a coarse honey, and is called Dibbs. Itis brought to markets in skins, has a sweet taste, and is much used by the people of all rank. Kaempfer in Amoenitt. exott. fasc. 2, p. 380: A large part of the grapes is reduced by boiling to a syrup, which takes the place of butter on the tables of the poor and, mixed with water, serves those who abstain from wine in place of wine. Olearius in der Persianischen und Moscowitischen Reisebeschreibung book 5, ch. 9, p. 577: Aus dem Moste machen die Perser einen Syrup, welchen sie Duschab nennen. Sie kochen den Most so lange, bis nur der sechste Theil davon übrig bleibt, und wie ein dickes Oel fliesst. Wenn er gebraucht werden soll, wird er mit Wasser und ein wenig Essig vermischt, welches sodann ein angenehmes Getränke giebt. Sie kochen auch bisweilen den Duschab so hart, dass man ihn schneiden kann. Die Reisenden pflegen ihn so trokken mitzunehmen, und im Wasser in ihrem Getränke zu zerlassen. Cf. below, note 8.

Similarly Suidas, under the word ἀκρίδας [akridas]: ἤσθιε δε ἀκριδας ὁ προδρομος καὶ μελι ἀγριον, ὁπερ ἀπο των δενδρων ἐπισυναγομενον μαννα τοις πολλοις προσαγορευεται· [ēsthie de akridas ho prodromos kai meli agrion, hoper apo tōn dendrōn episynagomenon manna tois pollois prosagoreuetai] the forerunner ate ἀκριδας [akridas] and wild honey, which is gathered from trees and is commonly called manna. This view was also adopted by Wesseling on Diodor. Sic. But J. D. Michaelis, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 4, p. 1134, contends that יער and יערה are honey dripping from trees, which Diodorus Siculus, Biblioth. book 19, §94, calls μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion]. He is moved chiefly by this argument: in 1 Sam. XIV, 27. (var. 25. 26.) the Israelites, pursuing the Philistines through a forest, are said to have come upon a large tract covered with honey, whereas bees' honey certainly does not cover wide estates. He adds that in v. 27 Jonathan is said to have dipped his staff ביערת הדבש, and that it is not credible that someone who had disturbed with a staff the honey stores of bees placed on the ground would have gone unpunished. But it is nowhere said that a large tract was covered with honey; in verse 25 we read only these words: ויהי דבש על-פני השדה, honey was found on the ground, which had flowed down from hollows of trees or from clefts in rocks (cf. below, notes 5, 6). Into this honey lying on the ground Jonathan could dip his staff with impunity. — Much less acceptable is the opinion of Rabbi Nathan the Ishmaelite, who interprets יערת דבש as forest of honey, understanding by that name a thicket of sugar canes; this opinion was followed by R. Solomon Jarchi, and after him defended by Cocceius and Gussetius in their Lexicons and by Hiller in Hierophyt. vol. 2, p. 203–204. But Michaelis rightly observes, in the Supplemm. p. 1135, that this meaning fits neither 1 Sam. XIV, 27. nor Cantic. V, 1. "There are sugar canes in Eretz Yisrael, I admit, but in the place where the battle with the Philistines was fought there were no thickets of sugar canes or of other reeds, much less such large ones that a victorious people pursuing the vanquished could have entered them. Further, and this alone is enough, who, travelling through sugar canes, could dip a staff into them and bring honey extracted from them to his mouth?" — Let the meaning honeycomb stand, then, which the passage Cantic. V, 1. virtually demands: I have eaten יַעְרִי עִם דִּבְשִׁי, my honeycomb with my honey, as the Vulgate translator has it. Cf. also Velthusen's commentary on this passage of the Song, p. 392.
